title: MCA Settlement Success Rates: How to Evaluate the Evidence
excerpt: How to assess MCA settlement claims: define completion, include fees and unresolved accounts, and compare written proposals with an affordable cash-flow plan.
contentMd:
## Can an MCA settlement success rate predict your result?

Not without knowing how it was measured. A credible rate needs a defined group of accounts, a reporting period, a clear meaning of “settled,” and an explanation of fees, withdrawals, and unresolved cases. A selected testimonial or a quoted discount cannot answer those questions.

BDI has not published a verified dataset supporting an industry-wide MCA settlement success rate or average discount. We therefore do not present a percentage as the result you should expect. Your planning should use the actual agreements, available cash, and written creditor proposals.

**Editorial correction — October 10, 2026:** An earlier version of this page presented precise closure, discount, and timeline figures without an identified dataset. Those figures have been removed. The examples below are hypothetical arithmetic, not BDI results or industry benchmarks.

## Define what “success” counts

Ask the provider to distinguish these outcomes:

| Outcome | What the record should show |
| --- | --- |
| Offer received | A proposed amount and deadline; acceptance and funding may still be outstanding |
| Settlement agreed | A signed agreement specifying obligations and conditions |
| Settlement completed | Required payments made and completion documented under the agreement |
| Payment modified | A revised schedule; the total obligation may remain unchanged |
| Unresolved or withdrawn | The account remains outside the completed-settlement count |

A business with four accounts and one completed settlement is not the same result as a business with all four resolved. Ask whether a headline measures businesses, individual accounts, or dollars of enrolled balances.

## Seven questions behind a success-rate claim

1. **Who is in the denominator?** All enrolled accounts, only completed clients, or only accounts that received offers?
2. **What dates are covered?** Request the enrollment period, measurement date, and follow-up duration.
3. **What counts as completion?** A verbal offer, signed agreement, first installment, or documented final payment?
4. **What happened to everyone else?** Identify open cases, cancellations, withdrawals, litigation, and payment modifications separately.
5. **Are fees included?** Separate payments to creditors from provider fees, legal costs, account fees, and other charges.
6. **How is the average calculated?** An account-count average and a balance-weighted average can tell different stories.
7. **What evidence supports the claim?** Ask for a written methodology and appropriately redacted supporting records or an independent review. Private client identities are not necessary.

These questions are a method for evaluating a claim. They do not establish that any particular provider has inaccurate results.

## Why the denominator changes the headline

Consider a **hypothetical** group of 100 enrolled accounts. At the reporting date, 60 have completed settlements, 20 remain open, 10 have withdrawn, and 10 have payment modifications.

Completed settlements represent 60% of all enrolled accounts. Reporting 100% by looking only at the 60 completed settlements would omit the unresolved and other outcomes. Neither number predicts whether your own creditors will accept an offer.

A useful report gives the count in each category and the time allowed for completion. It should not silently treat open accounts as failures or remove them to improve the headline.

## Calculate savings after fees

This is a **hypothetical illustration**, not an expected settlement:

| Item | Illustration |
| --- | ---: |
| Verified starting balance | $100,000 |
| Payments required by completed settlement | $60,000 |
| Provider and legal fees | $10,000 |
| Total paid to complete the arrangement | $70,000 |
| Net reduction before any tax consequences | $30,000, or 30% |

The creditor discount is 40%, but the reduction after the illustrated fees is 30%. Additional charges or unresolved balances would change the result.

Use the same starting-balance date for each proposal. Do not compare one offer against the original purchased amount and another against a later payoff balance.

The [IRS explains that canceled debt can be taxable, with exceptions and exclusions](https://www.irs.gov/taxtopics/tc431). Ask a tax professional how the actual transaction and business structure affect the calculation; a marketing savings percentage is not a tax estimate.

## A lower payment is not necessarily a settlement

Read the proposed document before counting an outcome. For example, [Forward Financing’s revenue-based contract guide](https://www.forwardfinancing.com/resources/forward-revenue-based-financing-contract-highlights/) describes reconciliation refunds that do not reduce the total amount sold. That is different from an agreement accepting less to resolve an obligation.

For your own account, distinguish a payment adjustment, reconciliation, refinance, and reduced-balance settlement. Identify the actual product and creditor; frequent withdrawals alone do not make a business loan an MCA.

## Build a creditor-by-creditor cash plan

Prepare a schedule showing each agreement, current claimed balance, payment dates, available settlement cash, fees, and any deadlines. Include a scenario in which an offer is declined or delayed.

Ask the adviser to explain which parts of the plan require creditor agreement, how your funds are held, what happens if the plan cannot be completed, and which services the fee covers. A projected discount is not money available to pay payroll.

Do not change payments solely to chase a claimed success rate. Have the actual contract and any litigation deadlines reviewed by qualified counsel before a decision that could create default consequences. BDI provides consulting, not legal representation.

## Questions to answer before enrolling

**Can anyone promise that every creditor will settle?** A proposed program does not itself establish creditor acceptance. Request account-specific written agreements and distinguish an estimate from a binding commitment.

**How long should settlement take?** This page does not establish a typical completion time. Ask for proposed milestones, dependencies, and the consequences of delay. A timeline for one selected case is not a distribution of outcomes.

**Which comparison matters most?** Compare the complete cash cost, the obligations actually resolved, the remaining risks, and the affordability of the schedule.
